query:
Systematic prior-art survey: closed-loop, automated, or algorithm-driven optimization of EBSD (electron backscatter diffraction) data-processing and indexing parameters.

Specifically map what has been published on:
1. Automated or optimizer-driven tuning of EBSD pattern-processing or indexing parameters (background correction, binning, neighbour averaging, Hough transform settings such as band count / rho-theta smoothing, dictionary indexing settings), using Bayesian optimization, Gaussian processes, genetic/evolutionary algorithms, grid/random search, or reinforcement learning.
2. Feedback loops that re-index stored raw EBSD patterns and use quality metrics (confidence index CI, image quality IQ, mean angular deviation / fit, normalized cross-correlation NCC) as an objective function to select the next parameter set.
3. Work that optimizes against GRAIN-LEVEL or microstructure-level outcomes (grain count stability vs misorientation threshold, fraction of speckle/wild grains, grain boundary integrity, fraction of pixels altered by cleanup) rather than only per-pixel pattern-level scores — i.e., multi-objective or constrained optimization of EBSD processing.
4. Hybrid indexing strategies (Hough first, dictionary indexing on low-quality residue) and any published AUTOMATED criteria for when to escalate from Hough to dictionary/pattern-matching indexing.
5. Software tools or frameworks claiming autonomous, self-driving, or human-out-of-the-loop EBSD post-processing or characterization workflows, including anything connecting post-processing results back to SEM acquisition-parameter recommendations (beam current, dwell time, step size).

For each area, identify the closest published work with citations, state clearly what it does and does NOT automate, and conclude with an assessment of which of the five areas remain unclaimed gaps in the literature.

A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available

        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care

info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal

    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.

    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Systematic prior-art survey: closed-loop, automated, or algorithm-driven optimization of EBSD (electron backscatter diffraction) data-processing and indexing parameters.

Specifically map what has been published on:
1. Automated or optimizer-driven tuning of EBSD pattern-processing or indexing parameters (background correction, binning, neighbour averaging, Hough transform settings such as band count / rho-theta smoothing, dictionary indexing settings), using Bayesian optimization, Gaussian processes, genetic/evolutionary algorithms, grid/random search, or reinforcement learning.
2. Feedback loops that re-index stored raw EBSD patterns and use quality metrics (confidence index CI, image quality IQ, mean angular deviation / fit, normalized cross-correlation NCC) as an objective function to select the next parameter set.
3. Work that optimizes against GRAIN-LEVEL or microstructure-level outcomes (grain count stability vs misorientation threshold, fraction of speckle/wild grains, grain boundary integrity, fraction of pixels altered by cleanup) rather than only per-pixel pattern-level scores — i.e., multi-objective or constrained optimization of EBSD processing.
4. Hybrid indexing strategies (Hough first, dictionary indexing on low-quality residue) and any published AUTOMATED criteria for when to escalate from Hough to dictionary/pattern-matching indexing.
5. Software tools or frameworks claiming autonomous, self-driving, or human-out-of-the-loop EBSD post-processing or characterization workflows, including anything connecting post-processing results back to SEM acquisition-parameter recommendations (beam current, dwell time, step size).

For each area, identify the closest published work with citations, state clearly what it does and does NOT automate, and conclude with an assessment of which of the five areas remain unclaimed gaps in the literature.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Concurrently, at these same scales, the deformation fields that develop during mechanical loading can be highly heterogeneous. Spatially correlated measurements of 3D microstructure and the ensuing deformation fields at the micro-scale would provide highly valuable insight into the relationship between microstructure and macroscopic mechanical response. Abstract:
Over the last two decades, platinum group metals (PGMs) and their alloys have dominated as the materials of choice for electrodes in long-term implantable neurostimulation and cardiac rhythm management devices due to their superior conductivity, mechanical and chemical stability, biocompatibility, corrosion resistance, radiopacity, and electrochemical performance. Despite these benefits, PGM manufacturing processes are extremely costly, complex, and challenging with potential health hazards. Additionally, the volatility in PGM prices and their high supply risk, combined with their scarce concentration of approximately 0.01 ppm in the earth's upper crust and limited mining geographical areas, underscores their classification as critical raw materials, thus, their effective recovery or substitution worldwide is of paramount importance. Since postmortem recovery from deceased patients and/or refining of PGMs that are used in the manufacturing of the electrodes and microelectrode arrays is extremely rare, challenging, and highly costly, therefore, substitution of PGM-based electrodes with other biocompatible materials that can yield electrochemical performance values equal or greater than PGMs is the only viable and sustainable solution to reduce and ultimately substitute the use of PGMs in long-term implantable neurostimulation and cardiac rhythm management devices. In this article, we demonstrate for the first time how the novel technique of "reactive hierarchical surface restructuring" can be utilized on titanium-that is widely used in many non-stimulation medical device and implant applications-to manufacture biocompatible, low-cost, sustainable, and high-performing neurostimulation and cardiac rhythm management electrodes. We have shown how the surface of titanium electrodes with extremely poor electrochemical performance undergoes compositional and topographical transformations that result in electrodes with outstanding electrochemical performance.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Deep learning (DL) is one of the fastest-growing topics in materials data science, with rapidly emerging applications spanning atomistic, image-based, spectral, and textual data modalities. DL allows analysis of unstructured data and automated identification of features. The recent development of large materials databases has fueled the application of DL methods in atomistic prediction in particular. In contrast, advances in image and spectral data have largely leveraged synthetic data enabled by high-quality forward models as well as by generative unsupervised DL methods. In this article, we present a high-level overview of deep learning methods followed by a detailed discussion of recent developments of deep learning in atomistic simulation, materials imaging, spectral analysis, and natural language processing. For each modality we discuss applications involving both theoretical and experimental data, typical modeling approaches with their strengths and limitations, and relevant publicly available software and datasets. We conclude the review with a discussion of recent cross-cutting work related to uncertainty quantification in this field and a brief perspective on limitations, challenges, and potential growth areas for DL methods in materials science.</jats:p>

Abstract:
A microstructure analytics and 3D reconstruction software package, DREAM.3D, was integrated as a module into a cloud-based platform, BisQue. Parallelization of DREAM.3D module executions and the ability to parameterize pipeline variables over a range of values have led to insights about the grain segmentation misorientation tolerance in TriBeam-collected 3D EBSD datasets of additively manufactured materials with complex anisotropic microstructures. Furthermore, a comparison in grain size measurements was made between standard 2D metallographic slices and 3D measures using BisQue’s parallelized DREAM.3D module executions. The direction of cloud-based data infrastructure and the prospects for impact in material science are also discussed.

Abstract:

 This study comprehensively reviews recent advances in the digital reconstruction of polycrystalline materials. Digital reconstruction serves as both a representative volume element for multiscale modelling and a source of quantitative data for microstructure characterisation. Three main types of digital reconstruction in polycrystalline materials exist: (i) experimental reconstruction, which links processing-structure-properties-performance by reconstructing actual polycrystalline microstructures using destructive or non-destructive methods; (ii) physics-based models, which replicate evolutionary processes to establish processing-structure linkages, including cellular automata, Monte Carlo, vertex/front tracking, level set, machine learning, and phase field methods; and (iii) geometry-based models, which create ensembles of statistically equivalent polycrystalline microstructures for structure-properties-performance linkages, using simplistic morphology, Voronoi tessellation, ellipsoid packing, texture synthesis, high-order, reduced-order, and machine learning methods. This work reviews the key features, procedures, advantages, and limitations of these methods, with a particular focus on their application in constructing processing-structure-properties-performance linkages. Finally, it summarises the conclusions, challenges, and future directions for digital reconstruction in polycrystalline materials within the framework of computational materials engineering.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Systematic discrepancies persist between results from grain size measurement standards, such as ASTM E 112 and ASTM E 2627, when different imaging techniques and analysis methods are used. The source of these discrepancies may be differences in imaging physics, resolution limits, grain boundary definitions, post-processing practices, or combinations thereof. Geometric distortions and drift effects in scanning electron microscope imaging are systematically modeled using synthetic microstructures to assess their impact on electron backscatter diffraction-based grain size measurement accuracy. Standard methods are compared to a lesser-known method, the Triple Point Count (TPC). Most distortion types introduce smaller biases than the expected accuracy of the methods under typical imaging conditions. TPC provides consistent performance across varying resolutions and sampling conditions. This provides further evidence that reported discrepancies are largely driven by an assumption made in the estimate for converting intercept measurements to ASTM grain size numbers, as recently reported by Evans et al.</jats:p>

Mohadeseh", title = "High-strength additively manufacturable Al-Zr-Er-Ni alloys with high as-built ductility and thermal stability", year = "2025", journal = "Unknown journal", month = "May", doi = "10.21203/rs.3.rs-6558867/v1", url = "https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-6558867/v1", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC" } Abstract: Abstract

Additively manufactured (AM) aluminum (Al) alloys with high as-built ductility offer sustainability, enhanced load-bearing performance, and resistance to residual-stress-induced failure. However, most commercial AM Al alloys have very limited ductility. In this study, we designed an AM Al-1.63Zr-2.38Er-1.34Ni (wt. %) alloy with 16% as-built ductility, while not introducing nanopowders or expensive scandium (Sc) to the formulation. We revealed that Al3Zr accounted for 65% of cavitation in the as-built condition by SEM characterizations. With calculation of phase diagram (CALPHAD)-based integrated computational materials engineering (ICME) simulations, we found that at each Er composition, Zr must not exceed the threshold required to act as a reservoir for the L12 phase transformation (needed for high strength) during aging. An optimized composition was identified following the guideline of Zr = 1.07 × Er; this composition enhances the ductility from 0.9% to 16% (1600% increase) in the as-built sample, while only decreasing strength by 27% compared to the benchmark alloy. The strength is preserved even after aging for 48 hours at 400°C.

Since then, a technological revolution has occurred in the quality, rate detection, and analysis of these diffractions patterns. The next revolution in EBSD is the ability to directly utilize the information rich diffraction patterns in a high-throughput manner. Aided by machine learning techniques, this new methodology is, as demonstrated herein, capable of accurately separating phases in a material by crystal symmetry, chemistry, and even lattice parameters with fewer human decisions. Abstract:
<jats:p>Due to its unique benefits over conventional subtractive manufacturing, additive manufacturing methods continue to attract interest in both academia and industry. One such method is called Cold Spray Additive Manufacturing (CSAM), a solid-state coating deposition technology to manufacture repair metallic components using a gas jet and powder particles. CSAM offers low heat input, stable phases, suitability for heat-sensitive substrates, and high deposition rates. However, persistent challenges include porosity control, geometric accuracy near edges and concavities, anisotropy, and cost sensitivities linked to gas selection and nozzle wear. Interdisciplinary research across manufacturing science, materials characterisation, robotics, control, artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML) is deployed to overcome these issues. ML supports quality prediction, inverse parameter design, in situ monitoring, and surrogate models that couple process physics with data. To demonstrate the impact of AI and ML on CSAM, this study presents a systematic literature review to identify, evaluate, and analyse published studies in this domain. The most relevant studies in the literature are analysed using keyword co-occurrence and clustering. Four themes were identified: design for CSAM, material analytics, real-time monitoring and defect analytics, and deposition and AI-enabled optimisation. Based on this synthesis, core challenges are identified as small and varied datasets, transfer and identifiability limits, and fragmented sensing. Main opportunities are outlined as physics-based surrogates, active learning, uncertainty-aware inversion, and cloud-edge control for reliable and adaptable ML use in CSAM. By systematically mapping the current landscape, this work provides a critical roadmap for researchers to target the most significant challenges and opportunities in applying AI/ML to industrialise CSAM.</jats:p>

Abstract:
A comparison study of grain segmentation in 2D and 3D electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) measurements of polycrystalline materials, based on a misorientation threshold, is presented. Using Laguerre tessellations with orientation marks, a simulation study that demonstrates a different sensitivity of segmentation in the case of low angle and high angle grain boundaries is involved. Then two metallic materials measured by 3D EBSD are investigated concerning segmentation, and there are given some recommendations for the misorientation thresholds. Computational tools such as DREAM 3D software enable significant data evaluation that is completed by a five-parameter analysis of grain boundaries. K e y w o r d s: electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), grain boundaries, misorientation, tessellation

Received: 30 December 2018 / Accepted: 18 February 2019 / Published online: 22 March 2019

Abstract
A microstructure analytics and 3D reconstruction software package, DREAM.3D, was integrated as a module into a
cloud-based platform, BisQue. Parallelization of DREAM.3D module executions and the ability to parameterize pipeline
variables over a range of values have led to insights about the grain segmentation misorientation tolerance in TriBeam-
collected 3D EBSD datasets of additively manufactured materials with complex anisotropic microstructures. Furthermore,
a comparison in grain size measurements was made between standard 2D metallographic slices and 3D measures using
BisQue’s parallelized DREAM.3D module executions. The direction of cloud-based data infrastructure and the prospects
for impact in material science are also discussed.

Keywords Tomography · 3D materials science · Microstructure analytics · Cloud infrastructure · Additive manufacturing ·

      Abstract

     The emergence of commercial electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) equipment ushered in an era of information rich maps produced by
      determining the orientation of user-selected crystal structures. Since then, a technological revolution has occurred in the quality, rate detec-
        tion, and analysis of these diffractions patterns. The next revolution in EBSD is the ability to directly utilize the information rich diffraction
       patterns in a high-throughput manner. Aided by machine learning techniques, this new methodology is, as demonstrated herein, capable of
       accurately separating phases in a material by crystal symmetry, chemistry, and even lattice parameters with fewer human decisions. This
     work is the first demonstration of such capabilities and addresses many of the major challenges faced in modern EBSD. Diffraction patterns
       are collected from a variety of samples, and a convolutional neural network, a type of machine learning algorithm, is trained to autono-
      mously recognize the subtle differences in the diffraction patterns and output phase maps of the material. This study offers a path to
      machine learning coupled phase mapping as databases of EBSD patterns encompass an increasing number of the possible space groups,
      chemistry changes, and lattice parameter variations.

hard metal data collected previously [11]. We present a new methodology for SE-EBSD image
pair co-registration based on trainable Combination of Shifted Filter Responses filters and two-
dimensional Moving Least Squares method. Our approach and it’s validation relies on three
assumptions, 1) Each of our slices are planar, 2) SE images taken on the SEM, at 0° stage tilt,
are distortion free and 3) the approach validation was done on the reasonable expectation of
the large WC grains to have planar facets, which are reported elsewhere for similar CW-Co
systems [32,50,58–61] and are also seen in etched samples [32] and the abundance of WC
grains with straight grain edges or boundaries in the 2D images and EBSD analysis of polished
surfaces. The alignment of the corrected facets with the expected crystallographic planes was
further validation of the corrected 3D-EBSD data. This allowed 3D-EBSD data to be corrected
and used for quantitative analyses and 3D visualisation. This is applied to our hard metal case
study giving rise to the following conclusions:
• The cumulative long-range distortions, in the EBSD maps compared to the reference SE
   images, were quantified as being of the order of up to 10 m across a 200 × 200 m area
   section.  They were found to significantly affect the shapes of individual grains in 2D
   leading to significant errors in grain morphologies in 3D. We should note that the distortion
   corrections effect the shape of the grains and not the orientation.
•  Curtaining effects were observed on the serial sections and the topography was measured
   using confocal microscopy and reported in our earlier paper  [11], but the confocal
   microscopy measurements were not used in the correction methods here and is a subject of
   future work. However, due to the inclined angle of incidence lead to significant distortions
   (a few pixels, up to 0.3 m) [11] of EBSD maps given that the grains are of the order of the
   grid used for long-range correction, these distortions required short-range correction. Here
   an attempt has been made to use to correct the distortions in a 3D-EBSD dataset of a hard
   metal case, with respect to the SE images and the expectation of the 3D shapes of the hard
   metal grains from the chemical extracted method as discussed earlier in section 3.
• 3D visualisation clearly showed that the volume of reconstructed microstructure using the
  raw data was severely deformed, where surface topography for a flat facet can be as high as
   3.3 m.
•  Using only the long-range correction, the topography for a planar facet, of a large well-
   defined WC grain, was reduced to 2.9 m and the normal of the planar facet lay within about
   10° – 20° crystallographic positioning error.
• By applying the short-range corrections, the distortion corrections reduced the maximum
   roughness of the planar facet surface topography to 0.4 m and the misalignment of the
   surface of the grain facets to their respective crystallographic planes were reduced to about
   7° – 12°.
These types of distortion correction algorithms are required to improve the accuracy of the
EBSD maps. In this study the accuracy was based on the roughness of the reconstructed grainfacets, where a suitable material was chosen that the large WC grains are known to have planar
facets. Going forwards more automated procedures need to be developed so that large area
EBSD maps can be routinely corrected and a more robust measure of accuracy needs to be
developed. This is especially important when reconstructing 3D data because registry from
layer to layer is important if features are not to be introduced into the reconstructed grain
morphologies. The correction methods outlined could be applied for 2D EBSD maps and 3D
EBSD maps collected at different length-scales using other SST methods, e.g. mechanical
sectioning, SEM microtome, FIB-SEM tomography and  the more  recently developed
techniques developed for large area milling such as BIB, plasma and laser technologies
[15,16,68]. Furthermore, smart sampling techniques may be used for measuring accurate 3D
shapes with only the imaging data and reduce the time required  for orientation data
measurement.
• While the methods described above quantify and correct for in plane distortion, work also
   needs to be done to correct for the errors caused by uneven slice thickness during 3D
   reconstruction for visualisation to account for the actual spacing and misalignment of the
   successive layers in 3D-EBSD stacks.  This effect has previously been shown to be
   significant [11].  However, use of the topography information gathered by confocal
   microscopy for correction  is not  trivial and requires further work to incorporate the
   topography measurements into the 3D visualisation software. This requires the software to
  be able to handle non-orthogonal layers, which is not the case at the moment and is the
   subject of future work.

## 4. winiarski2021correctionofartefacts pages 4-6 (Context ID: pqac-00000009)

lity of the data can be compromised, such as in cases where there is
poor pattern quality, low signal to noise and signal to background ratios, multiple phases with
low symmetry, pseudo-symmetry and complex  crystal  structures and highly deformed
microstructures. This means EBSD data are often mapped at a dwell time per pixel of around
one to three orders of magnitude longer than SE imaging, which results in acquisition times of
hundreds of minutes per map.

     As a result large area scans can be undertaken rapidly by SE imaging, where image
distortions and drift can be kept to less than a pixel [10], by using a combination of suitable
beam dwell time, image pixel resolution and high enough magnification to minimise lens
distortions, where applications can be found in digital image correlation (DIC) techniques [33–
36]. However, acquiring an EBSD map can be much slower, therefore the electron beam or
the sample are prone to drifts away from the assumed position leading to long-range image
distortions during the acquisition of an EBSD map [1,37,38].  Furthermore, SE images are
usually taken at 0° stage tilt or incidence angle, while EBSD maps are taken at 70° stage tilt or
incidence angle. Therefore, the EBSD maps have 1/cosine(70°) or 2.9 times smaller beam
spacing or deflection in the direction perpendicular to the tilt axis in order to generate an
equidistant grid of measurements points on the sample surface. This results in almost a
threefold degradation in spatial resolution and increase of any effect from drift or ‘long-range
distortion’, furthermore it accentuates the distortion from topographic features or ‘short-range
distortion’, in the EBSD maps [12]. Thus, these distortion exaggerations are minimised during
SE imaging at 0° incidence angle.  This is also one of the advantages of the relatively new
technique of transmission EBSD (t-EBSD) or transmission Kikuchi diffraction (TKD), where
the sample is usually back tilted only between 0°-20° [39–42]. New approaches to EBSD
analysis, such as the ‘Dictionary based indexing’ [43,44] or smart acquisition [45] promise
faster acquisition times without compromising EBSD indexing rates, because either lower
quality EBSD patterns and faster EBSD mapping speeds can be used or already utilizes other
SEM imaging modes taken at higher speeds and requires less sampling points. Nevertheless,
EBSD analysis will continue to be much slower than conventional image acquisition and thus
more susceptible to drifts.
In a previous paper introducing serial section broad ion beam tomography we identified
distortions in large area 2D EBSD maps [11].  It was shown that these can seriously affect the
interpretation of 3D EBSD datasets if uncorrected through an exemplar study of the 3D
microstructure of WC-Co hard metals.  In this follow-up paper we return to this problem to
examine the nature and to quantify the magnitude of the long-range and short-range distortions
associated with acquiring large area 2D EBSD data. All imaging modes in the SEM can have
distortions, however to correct for the large distortions encountered in the EBSD maps we
assume that SE images are distortion free compared to the EBSD maps.  Furthermore, we
propose methods for correcting both of long and short-range distortions by comparing EBSD
maps to SE images. Our proposed methods utilise COSFIRE, Combination of Shifted Filter
Responses filters [46] and Moving Least Squares (MLS) rigid deformation method for digital
image morphing [47]. The aim of this paper is to raise awareness of these artefacts which are
largely neglected at present, to quantify them and to show the benefits of their correction. This
paper is not aimed at proposing the best method of correction, nor comparing the merits of
specific correction approaches, but rather to encourage a greater focus on developing such
methods going forwards.
     By way of a case study, this paper focuses on distortions associated with collecting
relatively large volume serial section data on WC-Co hard metals (or cermets). They are used
for machining, cutting, mining and drilling and are challenging because they contain a high
fraction of a ceramic phase (i.e. the WC grains) held together a ductile metallic phase (i.e. theCo).  The mechanical properties of cemented carbides strongly depend on the size and
morphology of the WC grains [48,49]. Abnormal grain growth (AGG) can have a detrimental
effect on the mechanical properties of cermets, since these oversized grains (typically > 10 -
30 µm) act as nucleation points for cracking, breakage and drill bit failure. The mechanism for
AGG is not yet sufficiently understood. Some attempts have been made to simulate AGG in
cemented carbide verified with experimental work and 2D analyses [50], but the plethora of
information that can be extracted from 3D analyses allows the opportunity to much more fully
study the AGG phenomenon.  It must be noted here that there are non-destructive techniques
available to study AGG during in-situ heating [51,52], however the resolution of these
techniques are presently about 1 m. Although FIB-SEM based techniques are destructive,
but are able to resolve volumes in 3D in nanometer resolution. Large area plasma FIB [25],
BIB-SEM [16], laser-PFIB-SEM [24] or PFIB spin milling methods [27] are needed to capture
data over microstructurally relevant large volumes. As a result, such EBSD data provides a
good case for quantification and correction of long and short-range corrections described in
this paper.





2.  Experimental procedure and SE-EBSD image pair co-registration

     As mentioned above, the focus of the current paper is on the quantification of long and
short-range distortions associated with large area EBSD mapping and methods for their
correction rather than on making serial sectioning experiments per se. To this end we return to
the 3D EBSD dataset collected by serial section BIB for the WC-Co hardmetal sample
described in [11].

          Sample

      The material studied was a Tungsten carbide and Cobalt (WC-Co) hardmetal containing
11 mass % Co and having the average grain diameter of 5 m [53]. The alloy was produced by
Marshalls Hard Metals Ltd using conventional powder metallurgical methods.  Tungsten
carbide (WC) has a hexagonal crystal structure with lattice parameters a=2.9Å and c=2.83Å.
The stable Cobalt (Co) phase has a cubic crystal structure with a lattice parameter size a=3.56Å.




          Broad ion beam sectioning
      The experimental BIB serial sectioning workflow followed in this study is described in
detail in a companion paper [11]. In essence, the sample was manually passed between a Gatan,
Ilion broad ion beam system and a dual beam FEI NOVA600i FIB-SEM.  The milling
conditions were 5 kV, 60 A with 20 minutes mill time per slice, where the average slice
thickness was 700 nm. After each material removal step a secondary electron (SE) image of
the surface was collected using the SEM at 0° sample tilt, after which the crystallographic
information is collected by EBSD mapping at 70° sample tilt, to form SE-EBSD image pairs.
The quality of Ar+ ion polish achieved by with the Ilion BIB results in a very good surface for
EBSD analysis without significant damage or phase transformation facilitating high indexing
rates (above 90%). The co-registration of successive images was achieved using markers made
by FIB [11].         SE-EBSD image pairs

stitching multiple scanned areas using the stage [6–8]. Although the size of the maps analysed
here are relatively modest compared to the largest ones reported elsewhere the distortion
corrections applied here are applicable to much larger areas too. The EBSD maps used in this
work were acquired at 200 nm step size with map size of 205 × 177 m (1024 × 884 pixels)

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Area | Closest published work(s) | What is automated | Objective/criterion | What is explicitly not automated | Gap assessment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Optimizer-driven tuning of EBSD pattern-processing or indexing parameters | **Closest demonstrated EBSD parameter sweep:** Polonsky et al. 2019 parameterized DREAM.3D reconstruction variables and swept grain-segmentation misorientation tolerance over 0.1–10° in 0.1° increments, generating 100 reconstructions; **nearby but different:** Zhu et al. 2022 is only available here as metadata for “global optimization algorithms” applied to orientation/pattern-center/deformation extraction, so it should be treated as adjacent prior art, not verified from text in this record; **nearby non-tuning automation:** Kaufmann et al. 2020 CNN phase mapping automates phase recognition from patterns rather than tuning EBSD processing settings (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005) | Automated batch execution / parameterization of reconstruction pipelines in BisQue+DREAM.3D; CNN-based direct phase classification from patterns in Kaufmann 2020 (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000004) | Polonsky used reconstruction-level metrics: fraction of “good” CI-masked voxels retained and total grain count, selecting an elbow/balance point at 2.0°; Kaufmann targets phase-map fidelity qualitatively against known microstructure/EDS, not optimizer search (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000005) | No evidence here of Bayesian optimization, Gaussian processes, genetic/evolutionary algorithms, RL, random/grid search over **pattern** processing settings such as background correction, binning, neighbor averaging, Hough band count, rho-theta smoothing, or dictionary settings. Polonsky optimizes segmentation/reconstruction variables after indexing, not indexing settings themselves. Kaufmann does not tune EBSD parameters at all (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000005) | **Gap largely open.** Closest evidence is reconstruction-pipeline parameterization, not closed-loop optimizer-driven tuning of pattern-processing/indexing knobs. |
| 2. Feedback loops that re-index stored raw patterns using CI/IQ/MAD/NCC to choose next parameter set | **Closest proposal:** Shen et al. 2019 proposes combining fast CNN predictions with a confidence measure (quaternion norm) so that high-confidence points get neighborhood dictionary search and low-confidence points get full dictionary search; **related raw-pattern availability, not loop:** Stinville et al. 2022 notes raw .up2 patterns can be opened in EMsoft DI / EMSphInx, enabling reindexing in principle (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003) | Shen automates confidence estimation for each location and proposes routing subsequent dictionary matching effort based on confidence; raw pattern archival in Stinville enables offline reindexing workflows (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000003) | Quaternion norm as confidence proxy in Shen; no demonstrated CI/IQ/MAD/NCC-driven next-parameter selection loop in the gathered evidence (pqac-00000017) | Shen does **not** demonstrate an executed closed loop that iteratively changes indexing/processing parameters and re-indexes stored raw patterns to maximize CI/IQ/MAD/NCC/NCC-like objectives; it is a proposed hybrid search allocation strategy. Stinville provides data access, not autonomous optimization (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000003) | **Gap open.** Proposal-level hybrid confidence routing exists, but not a demonstrated feedback optimizer that selects the next EBSD parameter set from reindexed raw patterns. |
| 3. Optimization against grain-level or microstructure-level outcomes | **Closest demonstrated:** Polonsky et al. 2019 explicitly optimizes a grain-segmentation parameter against microstructure-level outcomes (grain count and retained good-data fraction); Staněk et al. 2020 compares 2D/3D segmentation sensitivity to misorientation threshold and shows strong threshold dependence, but not autonomous optimization (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) | Automated parallel reconstructions and post-processing counts in Polonsky; analytical comparison of threshold effects on segmentation in Staněk (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000010) | Grain count stability / avoidance of grain merging plus retained CI-masked voxel fraction in Polonsky; sensitivity of number of grains and segmentation discrepancies vs threshold in Staněk (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000011) | No demonstrated multi-objective or constrained optimization over broader grain-level cleanup outcomes such as speckle/wild-grain fraction, grain-boundary integrity, fraction of pixels altered by cleanup, or Pareto balancing across multiple EBSD post-processing stages. Polonsky is a one-parameter sweep with manually interpreted elbow criterion (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000012) | **Partially occupied, but narrow.** Grain-level optimization exists for segmentation tolerance; broader autonomous multi-objective EBSD post-processing remains a gap. |
| 4. Hybrid Hough-first / dictionary-on-residue and automated escalation criteria | **Closest published work:** Shen et al. 2019 explicitly proposes a hybrid strategy: CNN preliminary prediction plus confidence, then pattern matching only in a neighborhood for high-confidence points and full dictionary search for low-confidence points; this is the clearest automated escalation criterion in the gathered evidence. Sparks et al. 2024 and Winiarski et al. 2021 automate registration/distortion correction workflows but not Hough→dictionary escalation (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000000, pqac-00000008) | Automated confidence scoring and proposed routing of dictionary-search scope in Shen; automated image registration/distortion correction in Sparks/Winiarski (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000000, pqac-00000008) | Criterion in Shen is confidence from quaternion norm: high confidence → local neighborhood dictionary search; low confidence → full dictionary search (pqac-00000017) | No evidence in the gathered text of a **demonstrated** Hough-first then dictionary-on-low-quality-residue loop with automated escalation based on CI/IQ/MAD/NCC thresholds. Shen’s routing is proposed around CNN+dictionary, not Hough+dictionary, and not shown as an executed autonomous residue-reindexing pipeline (pqac-00000017) | **Mostly gap.** There is a close proposal for automated escalation, but not a demonstrated Hough-residue-to-dictionary autonomous workflow. |
| 5. Autonomous/self-driving EBSD post-processing or characterization workflows, including links back to SEM acquisition recommendations | **Closest workflow automation:** Sparks et al. 2024 automates sample/image registration steps, pattern-center fitting for every section, and alignment routines; Winiarski et al. 2021 automates SE–EBSD distortion correction and argues more automated procedures are needed; Burnett et al. 2016 demonstrates a fully automated serial-sectioning routine with tracking fiducials, but acquisition settings were experimentally chosen; Kaufmann et al. 2020 automates phase mapping from patterns (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000000, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000004) | Automated registration/warping, per-layer EBSD-to-BSE alignment, CI-threshold masks, pattern-center fitting per section, and automated serial sectioning with fiducial tracking; CNN inference for phase maps (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000004) | Workflow goals are geometric consistency, low inter-section misorientation, and corrected distortions; Burnett assesses equivalent quality via EBSD pattern quality/band contrast and indexing rate after experimentally selected settings (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000007) | No evidence here of a human-out-of-the-loop EBSD post-processing system that autonomously tunes post-processing/indexing parameters end-to-end, nor of a loop that feeds post-processing outcomes back to SEM acquisition parameters such as beam current, dwell time, or step size. Burnett explicitly determines acceptable milling current experimentally; Winiarski says more automated procedures still need to be developed (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008) | **Gap open.** Sub-workflow automation exists, but not a self-driving closed-loop EBSD characterization system that recommends or controls acquisition parameters from post-processing outcomes. |

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):

Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:

  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Systematic prior-art survey: closed-loop, automated, or algorithm-driven optimization of EBSD (electron backscatter diffraction) data-processing and indexing parameters.

Specifically map what has been published on:
1. Automated or optimizer-driven tuning of EBSD pattern-processing or indexing parameters (background correction, binning, neighbour averaging, Hough transform settings such as band count / rho-theta smoothing, dictionary indexing settings), using Bayesian optimization, Gaussian processes, genetic/evolutionary algorithms, grid/random search, or reinforcement learning.
2. Feedback loops that re-index stored raw EBSD patterns and use quality metrics (confidence index CI, image quality IQ, mean angular deviation / fit, normalized cross-correlation NCC) as an objective function to select the next parameter set.
3. Work that optimizes against GRAIN-LEVEL or microstructure-level outcomes (grain count stability vs misorientation threshold, fraction of speckle/wild grains, grain boundary integrity, fraction of pixels altered by cleanup) rather than only per-pixel pattern-level scores — i.e., multi-objective or constrained optimization of EBSD processing.
4. Hybrid indexing strategies (Hough first, dictionary indexing on low-quality residue) and any published AUTOMATED criteria for when to escalate from Hough to dictionary/pattern-matching indexing.
5. Software tools or frameworks claiming autonomous, self-driving, or human-out-of-the-loop EBSD post-processing or characterization workflows, including anything connecting post-processing results back to SEM acquisition-parameter recommendations (beam current, dwell time, step size).

For each area, identify the closest published work with citations, state clearly what it does and does NOT automate, and conclude with an assessment of which of the five areas remain unclaimed gaps in the literature.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>The development of high-fidelity mechanical property prediction models for the design of polycrystalline materials relies on large volumes of microstructural feature data. Concurrently, at these same scales, the deformation fields that develop during mechanical loading can be highly heterogeneous. Spatially correlated measurements of 3D microstructure and the ensuing deformation fields at the micro-scale would provide highly valuable insight into the relationship between microstructure and macroscopic mechanical response. They would also provide direct validation for numerical simulations that can guide and speed up the design of new materials and microstructures. However, to date, such data have been rare. Here, a one-of-a-kind, multi-modal dataset is presented that combines recent state-of-the-art experimental developments in 3D tomography and high-resolution deformation field measurements.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Over the last two decades, platinum group metals (PGMs) and their alloys have dominated as the materials of choice for electrodes in long-term implantable neurostimulation and cardiac rhythm management devices due to their superior conductivity, mechanical and chemical stability, biocompatibility, corrosion resistance, radiopacity, and electrochemical performance. Despite these benefits, PGM manufacturing processes are extremely costly, complex, and challenging with potential health hazards. Additionally, the volatility in PGM prices and their high supply risk, combined with their scarce concentration of approximately 0.01 ppm in the earth's upper crust and limited mining geographical areas, underscores their classification as critical raw materials, thus, their effective recovery or substitution worldwide is of paramount importance. Since postmortem recovery from deceased patients and/or refining of PGMs that are used in the manufacturing of the electrodes and microelectrode arrays is extremely rare, challenging, and highly costly, therefore, substitution of PGM-based electrodes with other biocompatible materials that can yield electrochemical performance values equal or greater than PGMs is the only viable and sustainable solution to reduce and ultimately substitute the use of PGMs in long-term implantable neurostimulation and cardiac rhythm management devices. In this article, we demonstrate for the first time how the novel technique of "reactive hierarchical surface restructuring" can be utilized on titanium-that is widely used in many non-stimulation medical device and implant applications-to manufacture biocompatible, low-cost, sustainable, and high-performing neurostimulation and cardiac rhythm management electrodes. We have shown how the surface of titanium electrodes with extremely poor electrochemical performance undergoes compositional and topographical transformations that result in electrodes with outstanding electrochemical performance.
