| 5. Autonomous/self-driving EBSD post-processing or characterization workflows, including links back to SEM acquisition recommendations | **Closest workflow automation:** Sparks et al. 2024 automates sample/image registration steps, pattern-center fitting for every section, and alignment routines; Winiarski et al. 2021 automates SE–EBSD distortion correction and argues more automated procedures are needed; Burnett et al. 2016 demonstrates a fully automated serial-sectioning routine with tracking fiducials, but acquisition settings were experimentally chosen; Kaufmann et al. 2020 automates phase mapping from patterns (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000000, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000004) | Automated registration/warping, per-layer EBSD-to-BSE alignment, CI-threshold masks, pattern-center fitting per section, and automated serial sectioning with fiducial tracking; CNN inference for phase maps (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000004) | Workflow goals are geometric consistency, low inter-section misorientation, and corrected distortions; Burnett assesses equivalent quality via EBSD pattern quality/band contrast and indexing rate after experimentally selected settings (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000007) | No evidence here of a human-out-of-the-loop EBSD post-processing system that autonomously tunes post-processing/indexing parameters end-to-end, nor of a loop that feeds post-processing outcomes back to SEM acquisition parameters such as beam current, dwell time, or step size. Burnett explicitly determines acceptable milling current experimentally; Winiarski says more automated procedures still need to be developed (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008) | **Gap open.** Sub-workflow automation exists, but not a self-driving closed-loop EBSD characterization system that recommends or controls acquisition parameters from post-processing outcomes. |


*Table: This table maps the closest published prior art found for the five requested EBSD automation areas, distinguishing demonstrated methods from proposals and from absent closed loops. It highlights that most evidence clusters around workflow automation and grain-segmentation parameter sweeps, not autonomous closed-loop tuning of indexing/processing parameters.*

## 1. Optimizer-driven tuning of pattern-processing or indexing parameters

### Closest demonstrated work: Polonsky et al. (2019)

Polonsky and colleagues integrated DREAM.3D into the cloud-based BisQue platform so that pipeline variables could be parameterized and executions parallelized. Their principal EBSD example varied the **post-indexing grain-segmentation misorientation tolerance** from 0.1° to 10° in 0.1° increments, producing 100 three-dimensional reconstructions while holding minimum-neighbor and minimum-defect-size settings fixed. They evaluated the fraction of CI-masked “good” voxels retained and total reconstructed grain count, then selected 2.0° from convergence/elbow behavior in the derivatives of those metrics. This is genuine automated parameter sweeping with microstructure-level evaluation. However, it operates on already indexed orientation data; the study states that raw EBSD patterns were not collected for that dataset. It therefore does **not** tune background correction, detector binning, neighbor averaging, Hough band count, Hough rho/theta smoothing, or dictionary-search settings, and it cannot re-index patterns under candidate settings. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000012)

### Adjacent work that should not be overread

Shen et al. developed CNN-based orientation indexing and optimized neural-network architecture/training for speed and prediction accuracy. The trained model indexes patterns directly and uses quaternion-norm deviation as a reliability measure. This replaces or supplements conventional indexing; it does not run Bayesian, evolutionary, grid, or reinforcement-learning search over conventional EBSD processing parameters. It also remains sensitive to experimental geometry and requires detector/setup parameters to be determined beforehand or accommodated through retraining. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017)

Kaufmann et al. automated phase classification from individual EBSD patterns with a CNN. The work reduces human decisions in phase mapping and outperforms conventional Hough-plus-user-selected phase/chemistry workflows in difficult examples. The “optimization” described for the conventional comparator was repeated **user adjustment** of EDS reference chemistry against a microstructure already known in advance, not an algorithmic search over EBSD settings. The CNN likewise classifies patterns rather than optimizing background, Hough, binning, or dictionary parameters. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005)

Global/evolutionary optimization has also been published for extracting or refining orientation, pattern center, and deformation state from pattern matching. That is important neighboring art: it establishes optimizer use **inside a per-pattern inverse problem**. It is not equivalent to an outer loop choosing data-processing/indexing hyperparameters from map-quality or grain-quality outcomes. The retrieved full-text evidence did not support treating such work as prior art for the broader closed-loop parameter-selection architecture.

**Assessment:** No verified publication was found that applies Bayesian optimization, a GP surrogate, genetic/evolutionary search, random/grid search, RL, or a comparable optimizer to the listed **pattern-processing and indexing knobs** and automatically selects the best configuration. Area 1 remains substantially open, aside from adjacent per-pattern refinement and post-indexing segmentation sweeps.

## 2. Re-indexing stored raw patterns in a metric-driven feedback loop

Stinville et al. provide a useful enabling precedent: their archived 3D dataset includes approximately 1.71 TB of raw `.up2` Kikuchi patterns, and the paper explicitly states that these can be opened and reprocessed with EMsoft dictionary indexing, EMSphInx spherical-pattern reindexing, or commercial EBSD software. The indexed files also expose IQ and CI. This demonstrates the technical availability of stored-pattern reindexing, but the paper is a dataset publication, not an optimizer: it does not generate candidate parameter sets, score them, or select the next experiment. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003)

Shen et al. provide the closest feedback-like decision rule. They propose obtaining a preliminary CNN orientation and confidence at every point, performing only a local dictionary search around high-confidence predictions, and performing a full dictionary search for low-confidence predictions. The confidence proxy is the norm of the predicted quaternion. This is automated computational routing, but it is not a demonstrated iterative loop over processing/indexing parameter sets, and it does not use CI, IQ, MAD/fit, or NCC to propose the next candidate configuration. (pqac-00000017)

Polonsky et al. use CI to define an initial mask of good voxels and assess how many remain after cleanup and segmentation. CI is therefore part of a reconstruction-level quality assessment, but it is not fed back to re-index raw patterns; indeed, raw patterns were unavailable in that example. (pqac-00000013)

**Assessment:** No demonstrated publication was found with the complete loop **candidate parameters → re-index stored raw patterns → compute CI/IQ/MAD/fit/NCC objective → choose the next parameter set → repeat**. Area 2 remains an unclaimed gap in the searched literature.

## 3. Grain- or microstructure-level objectives

This area has the strongest direct prior art, but it is narrow.

Polonsky et al. explicitly recognized that segmentation tolerance changes grain consolidation and retained data in opposite directions. Their two high-level metrics were total grain count and the fraction of initially CI-qualified voxels retained through reconstruction. They chose the lowest tolerance at which the changes in both quantities became approximately constant, analogous to an elbow criterion. This is a microstructure-level, effectively two-metric parameter-selection procedure rather than optimization of a per-pattern score. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000012)

Staněk et al. independently show why such objectives matter. They analyzed the dependence of 2D and 3D grain segmentation on misorientation threshold, including mean grain counts and the formation of erroneously merged giant grains. For one noisy experimental dataset, changing noise removal and excluding grains below eight voxels changed the detected population from more than one million grains to 74,579. This is a systematic sensitivity study and supplies possible grain-level observables, but it does not implement an autonomous optimizer or select cleanup parameters through a formal multi-objective rule. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011)

Neither publication demonstrates optimization across a broad EBSD-processing chain using objectives such as wild-grain/speckle fraction, boundary continuity or integrity, grain-count stability over threshold perturbations, fraction of pixels modified by cleanup, or a constraint on topology preservation. Polonsky varies essentially one segmentation parameter, keeps other settings fixed, and identifies a balance/elbow rather than computing a Pareto front or solving a constrained optimization problem. (pqac-00000013)

**Assessment:** Area 3 is **partially occupied**. A broad claim to “optimizing EBSD processing using grain-level outcomes” would encounter Polonsky et al. A narrower architecture that jointly tunes indexing and cleanup parameters using several topology- and intervention-aware grain objectives still appears open in the searched literature.

## 4. Hybrid Hough-first/dictionary-on-residue indexing

The closest automated escalation rule is Shen et al., but its first stage is a CNN rather than Hough indexing. Their proposed rule is explicit: high-confidence CNN results receive dictionary matching only near the preliminary orientation; low-confidence results receive full dictionary search. Thus, the publication anticipates confidence-triggered allocation of expensive pattern matching. It does not demonstrate a Hough-first pipeline, does not define residue using CI/IQ/MAD/NCC from Hough indexing, and does not report an executed end-to-end selective reindexing experiment. (pqac-00000017)

The same paper compares CNN and Hough indexing at different exposure times. CNN indexing produced a larger fraction of points below a 10° misorientation-error cutoff at high noise, whereas Hough was more accurate among the smaller subset it indexed correctly. This comparison motivates selective hybridization, but the reported hybrid suggestion remains CNN-to-dictionary rather than Hough-to-dictionary. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017)

Kaufmann et al. likewise replace conventional Hough phase assignment with CNN classification; they do not retain Hough as a first pass and selectively escalate failed pixels. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005)

**Assessment:** Confidence-triggered hybrid search is neighboring prior art, so a very broad claim to “use confidence to decide whether to run dictionary matching” is not open. However, no verified demonstration was found of **Hough first → automatically identify low-quality residue → dictionary/pattern-match only that residue**, particularly using an explicit CI/IQ/MAD/NCC or grain-context escalation criterion. Area 4 therefore remains mostly open in the requested Hough-specific form.

## 5. Autonomous EBSD workflows and acquisition feedback

Several publications automate substantial sub-workflows:

* **BisQue–DREAM.3D:** cloud execution, provenance, parallel pipeline runs, and range parameterization for 3D reconstruction. Parameters and ranges are supplied rather than autonomously discovered, and the demonstrated optimization begins after indexing. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000013)
* **Automated serial sectioning:** Burnett et al. describe a fully automated PFIB serial-section routine using automatically recognized tracking fiducials and repeated milling/imaging positions. Yet acceptable milling current was determined experimentally, and the authors state that systematic mapping of voltage/current space remained necessary. EBSD settings—including beam energy/current, dwell, binning, band count, and Hough settings—were fixed by the investigators rather than adapted from post-processing results. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007)
* **Automated registration and distortion correction:** Sparks et al. use automated sample alignment, pattern-center fitting for each section, CI thresholding, and optimizer-based multimodal registration. The optimizer maximizes an image-registration similarity metric and transforms maps; it does not alter EBSD indexing settings or SEM acquisition conditions. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000000)
* **SE–EBSD map correction:** Winiarski et al. automate aspects of co-registration and long-/short-range distortion correction using trainable filters and moving least squares. The paper explicitly concludes that more automated procedures and more robust accuracy measures still need development. It also discusses faster or smart acquisition as a prospect, not as a closed post-processing-to-acquisition controller. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000008)
* **CNN indexing/phase mapping:** Shen and Kaufmann automate inference from patterns, but training data, instrument calibration, phase standards, and/or model selection remain external; neither closes the loop to microscope settings. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000004)

No retrieved work used post-processing outcomes to recommend or automatically change **beam current, pattern dwell/exposure, detector binning, or spatial step size** for a subsequent SEM/EBSD acquisition. Burnett et al. come closest to connecting acquisition conditions with indexing rate and band contrast, but the comparison is an investigator-designed experiment, not a controller: selected ion currents are evaluated under fixed EBSD conditions and an acceptable current is chosen experimentally. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007)

**Assessment:** Automated components and scripted pipelines are well established, so “automated EBSD workflow” alone is not a gap. A genuinely autonomous, human-out-of-the-loop EBSD characterization system that interprets indexed/map/grain quality and then recommends or controls SEM acquisition parameters remains open in the searched literature.

## Consolidated gap assessment

1. **Optimizer-driven tuning of EBSD pattern-processing/indexing settings — open.** Neighboring art covers per-pattern inverse optimization, ML indexing, and post-indexing segmentation sweeps, but not outer-loop optimization of background, binning, averaging, Hough, or dictionary hyperparameters.
2. **Metric-driven iterative reindexing of stored raw patterns — open.** Raw-pattern reindexing is enabled and confidence-directed search is proposed, but the complete iterative objective loop was not found.
3. **Grain-level optimization — partially claimed.** Polonsky et al. directly cover segmentation-tolerance selection using retained-good-data fraction and grain count. Broad multi-objective, constrained, topology-aware optimization across indexing plus cleanup remains open.
4. **Automated hybrid escalation — partially anticipated, Hough-specific implementation open.** Shen et al. anticipate confidence-triggered local versus full dictionary search after CNN indexing. A demonstrated Hough-first, dictionary-on-residue workflow with formal escalation criteria was not found.
5. **Autonomous workflow with feedback to acquisition — open at the system level.** Serial sectioning, registration, reconstruction, correction, and ML inference are individually automated, but no end-to-end post-processing-to-SEM acquisition feedback system was found.

The most defensible unexplored combination is therefore: **repeated reindexing of archived raw patterns under optimizer-selected processing/indexing settings; joint pattern-, pixel-, and grain-level objectives with explicit cleanup/topology constraints; confidence- and grain-context-based escalation from Hough to dictionary matching; and translation of the optimized result into acquisition recommendations or microscope control.** None of the verified publications combines those elements into a closed, autonomous EBSD loop.

The paper addresses the inverse problem of orientation reconstruction from diffraction patterns and shows the method avoids traditional image processing steps (Gaussian filtering, Hough transforms, peak detection). reconstructing a crystallographic orientation from an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) pattern is achieved by solving an inverse problem, i.e. finding the inverse function which maps a given diffraction pattern to an orientation: g(X) = q

The most commonly used approach for orientation indexing from measured EBSD patterns utilizes image processing techniques including Gaussian filtering, Hough transforms, butterfly convolution, and peak detection for extracting Kikuchi bands
a quaternion norm metric provides a good confidence measure for assessing the quality of the reconstruction, without requiring ground truth information
The CNN based reconstruction method takes as little as 1 ms for orientation indexing, matching the highest practical scan rates, and thus enabling real-time orientation indexing

contexts.context: The Shen et al. 2019 paper discusses CNN-based orientation indexing for EBSD patterns. It addresses a key limitation: neural networks perform poorly on boundary points in the fundamental zone due to lack of crystallographic symmetry knowledge. The authors solve this by training multiple CNNs with transformed orientation spaces (effective fundamental zones). When using mean absolute error (MAE) loss, the network struggles because diffraction patterns from angles near boundaries (e.g., 0.001 and 1.999π) are visually similar but forced to predict very different values. The solution involves applying cubic symmetry operators to transform quaternions and create three additional effective fundamental zones where boundary points are repositioned to non-boundary locations, improving prediction accuracy. However, this excerpt does not contain information about low-confidence pattern handling, full dictionary search approaches, Polonsky et al. 2019 methods, evolutionary/global optimization techniques, or automated tuning of Hough parameters, background correction, binning settings, or feedback loops to SEM acquisition.

## Summary

This excerpt describes integration of DREAM.3D microstructure analysis software into BisQue, a cloud-based platform, to enable parallelized processing of 3D EBSD datasets from additively manufactured materials. The authors note that "reconstruction of 3D datasets is a complex process with many degrees of freedom" where "algorithms employed, and tolerances selected by the user...ultimately determine the quantitative data extracted." They highlight that "due to the long computation times required to process 3D data...it is impractical to explore the full parameter space by manually running reconstructions," and that "only several variables are adjusted by a user until a qualitatively acceptable reconstruction is attained. This process inherently imparts bias." The work demonstrates parameterizing "pipeline variables over a range of values" to study grain segmentation misorientation tolerance, but focuses on cloud infrastructure rather than automated optimization of EBSD indexing parameters or closed-loop feedback mechanisms using quality metrics.

# Summary

This excerpt addresses grain segmentation in 2D and 3D EBSD measurements of polycrystalline materials. The authors present a comparison study using misorientation thresholds (typical value: 5° in EDAX OIM software) to define grains as "sets of all points (voxels or pixels) with similar orientation, surrounded by a boundary of a given misorientation threshold." A critical finding is that "we may get different results of the segmentation in 2D and 3D, even if we use a fixed misorientation threshold." The paper uses "Laguerre tessellations with orientation marks" for simulation and employs "DREAM 3D software" for data evaluation. The discrepancy arises because "in a 2D cutting plane, two sets of voxels may be detected as two grains, while in the 3D case, all these points belong to one larger set" (particularly with nonconvex grains). The work demonstrates sensitivity differences between low-angle and high-angle grain boundary segmentation but does not address automated parameter optimization or feedback-loop indexing strategies.

# Summary

This 2020 paper introduces convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for autonomous EBSD phase mapping, addressing limitations of conventional Hough transform-based indexing. The authors note that "the Hough transform strips most of the information about the crystal structure and chemistry from the image" and results in "mis-classification of similar crystal structures." The work demonstrates CNN training to "autonomously recognize the subtle differences in the diffraction patterns and output phase maps" without extensive user input.

The paper acknowledges dictionary-based approaches (Park et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2015; Ram & De Graef, 2018) as solutions for phase differentiation, yet states these still rely on traditional Hough processing initially. The CNN methodology represents advancement toward "high-throughput manner" EBSD analysis with "fewer human decisions," suggesting movement toward autonomous workflows, though the excerpt does not detail feedback loops, grain-level optimization metrics, or systematic parameter tuning strategies.

This excerpt discusses comparison and alignment methodologies between EBSD and NF-HEDM crystallographic data, rather than automated optimization of EBSD parameters. Key findings include:

- Layer-to-layer misorientation thresholds of 3° used to define grain correspondence
- NF-HEDM data showed uniformly small misorientation angles (all below 0.05°), while EBSD sections exceeded 0.3° mean misorientation between sections
- Automated sample alignment routines and pattern center fitting enabled high consistency
- Per-layer empirical orientation alignment rotations reduced EBSD-HEDM misorientation: 95% of corresponding points achieved below 0.46° after alignment (mean 0.24°)
- Spherical harmonic indexing versus Hough indexing compared on raw EBSD patterns
- 46.2% noncorresponding points between EBSD and HEDM data identified, attributed to smaller grains/twins absent in HEDM reconstructions

This excerpt addresses **data registration and post-processing comparison** but does not address automated parameter optimization, feedback loops using quality metrics, or grain-level outcome optimization.

# Summary

This excerpt discusses CNN-based EBSD pattern indexing from Shen et al. (2019), comparing it to Hough transform and dictionary methods. Key findings:

**What it does:** Uses U-Net and CNN models to predict crystal orientations from EBSD patterns, achieving "50% of all points having <10° misorientation" at 1ms exposure versus "~15%" for Hough transform. The U-Net reconstructed 1×1 mm² scans in "17 min (4 ms per pattern)" on a MacBook Pro; retrained CNN in "5 min (1 ms per pattern)."

**What it does NOT automate:** The CNN requires "re-training the weights" when experimental geometry parameters change. The authors note that "a single neural network will not provide accurate predictions for all experimental geometry parameters." They suggest combining CNN with dictionary indexing but do not present automated criteria for method selection.

**Gap identified:** The excerpt proposes but does not implement "combining the two approaches: first apply CNN-based regression to obtain pre-[liminary results]"—indicating no published automated hybrid indexing strategy exists in this work.

# Summary

This excerpt describes a parameterization study of EBSD data post-processing, specifically optimizing the **misorientation tolerance parameter** for 3D grain segmentation. Key details:

- **Grain-level optimization metrics**: The work tracks two opposing trends—"number of grains" and "fraction of masked voxels"—as misorientation tolerance varies from 0.1° to 10° in 0.1° increments, generating "one-hundred 3D reconstructions."

- **Optimization method**: Uses the "Elbow method" via central difference derivatives to find the point where "both the change in fraction of masked data included and the change in the number of grains became constant," identifying 2.0° as optimal.

- **Microstructure-level focus**: Explicitly addresses avoiding "unnecessary merging of grains" and ensuring "grains with more reasonable grain morphologies," prioritizing grain-boundary integrity over per-pixel pattern scores.

- **Tool used**: BisQue framework enables automated parameterization and multi-reconstruction analysis.

- **Automation scope**: Parameter tuning is semi-automated but does NOT employ Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, or closed-loop feedback on raw EBSD patterns.

# Summary

This excerpt describes grain segmentation analysis using 3D-EBSD data on an AlMgSc alloy. The study examines how misorientation thresholds affect grain detection when comparing 2D versus 3D processing approaches. Key findings include:

- Three misorientation thresholds tested: 0.1°, 10%, and 15% of boundaries
- When the specimen thickness is ≥30 slices, 2D vs 3D processing differences become "significant"
- The difference becomes meaningful when "at least 10–15% of boundaries have misorientation lower than the threshold"
- Grain morphology plays minimal role; sample thickness is the main factor
- Processing parameters "firmly influence the number of detected grains" — using DREAM.3D with a 2° misorientation threshold detected 74,579 grains, but without noise filtering detected >1 million grains
- Noise substantially affects results; removing grains <8 voxels and applying filters is critical

The excerpt demonstrates **grain-level outcome variability** (grain count) dependent on processing parameter selection but does **not** describe automated optimization loops or feedback mechanisms for parameter tuning.

# Summary

This excerpt presents a CNN-based approach for EBSD orientation indexing by Shen et al. (2019). Key points:

**What is automated:** The paper develops "convolutional neural network approaches based on domain transform and transfer learning to reconstruct crystal orientations from electron backscatter diffraction patterns." The CNN models "index orientations as fast as the highest EBSD scanning rates" and are "robust to experimentally measured image noise."

**Quality assessment:** The authors "demonstrate that the quaternion norm metric is a strong indicator for assessing the reliability of the reconstructions."

**Limitations:** The CNN approach addresses orientation indexing speed but does not explicitly automate parameter tuning, feedback loops, grain-level optimization, hybrid indexing strategies, or closed-loop SEM acquisition control. Prior CNN work (Liu et al., Jha et al.) was "only trained and tested on simulated EBSD patterns," though this work extends to experimental data using "transfer learning" with "a small amount of experimental data."

This represents machine learning for pattern indexing but not systematic parameter optimization or autonomous workflow control.

This excerpt discusses EBSD (electron backscatter diffraction) analysis of WC-Co samples prepared with different ion-beam milling techniques, comparing results across BIB (Ar+), PFIB (Xe+), and FIB (Ga+) methods at varying currents and voltages.

Key findings: BIB at 6 kV produced "very high quality" EBSD patterns with 90% WC indexing and band contrast of 180/255. PFIB at 30 kV, 59 nA achieved 86% indexing with band contrast 108/255. FIB at 20 nA showed poor results (8% indexing, 40/255 band contrast), while FIB at 1 nA improved substantially (76% indexing, 94/255 contrast). The excerpt notes that "60× higher current (1 nA vs. 59 nA)" could be used in FIB versus PFIB to achieve "roughly equivalent quality" based on band contrast and indexing metrics. The authors acknowledge "considerable systematic work is required to map this parameter space" but do not describe automated optimization approaches or feedback loops for parameter selection.

# Summary

This excerpt addresses **3D-EBSD data correction**, not automated parameter optimization or indexing. It describes a methodology for correcting geometric distortions in EBSD maps using "trainable Combination of Shifted Filter Responses filters and two-dimensional Moving Least Squares method" applied to WC-Co hard metals.

Key findings:
- Quantified "long-range distortions...of the order of up to 10 μm across a 200 × 200 μm area"
- Long-range corrections reduced planar facet topography from 3.3 μm to 2.9 μm
- Short-range corrections further reduced roughness to 0.4 μm
- The authors acknowledge that "more automated procedures need to be developed so that large area EBSD maps can be routinely corrected"

**Relevance to survey**: This work does NOT address automated tuning of EBSD pattern-processing parameters, feedback loops with quality metrics, grain-level optimization objectives, hybrid indexing strategies, or autonomous workflows. It focuses narrowly on post-acquisition geometric correction, leaving all five survey areas unaddressed.

# Summary

The excerpt describes parameter optimization work on 3D EBSD data processing using the BisQue framework and DREAM.3D software. Key findings:

**Automated parameter tuning**: The authors systematically tested misorientation tolerance values from 0.1° to 10° (100 increments) on 3D reconstructions, using "two high-level metrics...the fraction of 'good' data, and the total number of grains found." They identified an optimal misorientation tolerance of 2.0° through derivative analysis balancing grain count stability and data retention (98.4% of masked data included, 899 grains identified).

**Grain-level outcomes**: The work explicitly optimizes against grain-level metrics rather than per-pixel scores—measuring fraction of retained data and total grain counts as reconstruction quality indicators.

**Coupled parameterization**: BisQue enables "automated generation of random samples of equal-sized subvolumes," allowing linked parameter sets.

However, the excerpt does **not** demonstrate: automated feedback loops re-indexing raw patterns, Bayesian/genetic algorithm optimization, hybrid indexing strategies, or autonomous SEM acquisition parameter recommendations.

# Summary

The excerpt discusses challenges in EBSD data acquisition and processing, particularly regarding spatial distortions in large-area maps. Key points:

**EBSD Acquisition Challenges:**
- EBSD requires "one to three orders of magnitude longer" dwell times than SE imaging, resulting in "acquisition times of hundreds of minutes per map"
- Maps acquired at 70° stage tilt experience "1/cosine(70°) or 2.9 times smaller beam spacing," causing "almost a threefold degradation in spatial resolution"
- Long-range and short-range distortions are "largely neglected at present"

**Emerging Solutions Mentioned:**
- "Dictionary based indexing" and "smart acquisition" promise "faster acquisition times without compromising EBSD indexing rates"
- Distortion correction methods using COSFIRE filters and Moving Least Squares (MLS) deformation are proposed

**Experimental Details:**
The WC-Co hardmetal case study used 200 nm step size, 4×4 binning (336×256 pixels), 25 ms indexing per point (40 Hz), achieving ">96%" indexing rate—notably slower than typical operation.

The excerpt emphasizes distortion as an understudied problem but does not address automated parameter optimization, feedback loops, or grain-level outcome optimization.

# Summary

The excerpt describes CNN-based approaches for EBSD pattern indexing and microstructure reconstruction. Key points:

**CNN Method:** Demonstrated "relatively fast" real-time reconstruction capability during scanning, but "not as accurate as the dictionary approach, which can reconstruct noisy data with high accuracy."

**Hybrid Strategy:** Proposes combining CNN and dictionary methods: "first apply CNN-based regression to obtain preliminary predictions and a measure of confidence for each location...For locations with high confidence reconstructions, run the pattern matching only in the neighborhood (e.g. 10+) of the preliminary results in the dictionary. For those with low confidence, run the full dictionary search."

**Confidence Metric:** Uses "quaternion norm as a measure of confidence" to assess reconstruction reliability and determine which indexing approach to apply.

**Domain Adaptation:** Employs U-Net and transfer learning to adapt CNNs trained on simulated patterns to experimental data, addressing simulation-experiment discrepancies through convolutional layer retraining.

The work addresses noise robustness and matching "EBSD scanning rates" but focuses on per-pattern indexing rather than grain-level optimization or automated parameter tuning.

Question: Systematic prior-art survey: closed-loop, automated, or algorithm-driven optimization of EBSD (electron backscatter diffraction) data-processing and indexing parameters.

Specifically map what has been published on:
1. Automated or optimizer-driven tuning of EBSD pattern-processing or indexing parameters (background correction, binning, neighbour averaging, Hough transform settings such as band count / rho-theta smoothing, dictionary indexing settings), using Bayesian optimization, Gaussian processes, genetic/evolutionary algorithms, grid/random search, or reinforcement learning.
2. Feedback loops that re-index stored raw EBSD patterns and use quality metrics (confidence index CI, image quality IQ, mean angular deviation / fit, normalized cross-correlation NCC) as an objective function to select the next parameter set.
3. Work that optimizes against GRAIN-LEVEL or microstructure-level outcomes (grain count stability vs misorientation threshold, fraction of speckle/wild grains, grain boundary integrity, fraction of pixels altered by cleanup) rather than only per-pixel pattern-level scores — i.e., multi-objective or constrained optimization of EBSD processing.
4. Hybrid indexing strategies (Hough first, dictionary indexing on low-quality residue) and any published AUTOMATED criteria for when to escalate from Hough to dictionary/pattern-matching indexing.
5. Software tools or frameworks claiming autonomous, self-driving, or human-out-of-the-loop EBSD post-processing or characterization workflows, including anything connecting post-processing results back to SEM acquisition-parameter recommendations (beam current, dwell time, step size).

For each area, identify the closest published work with citations, state clearly what it does and does NOT automate, and conclude with an assessment of which of the five areas remain unclaimed gaps in the literature.

# Systematic prior-art survey: closed-loop optimization of EBSD processing and indexing

## Scope and search interpretation

The survey distinguished four often-confounded categories: **(i)** optimization of pattern-processing or indexing parameters, **(ii)** algorithmic refinement of orientation or pattern-center estimates for a fixed pattern, **(iii)** automated post-indexing map cleanup/segmentation, and **(iv)** automation of acquisition or registration. Only the first category squarely satisfies area 1; automation in the other categories is relevant as neighboring prior art but does not establish a closed-loop EBSD indexing optimizer.

Searches covered EBSD with Bayesian optimization, Gaussian processes, evolutionary/genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, grid/random search, reinforcement learning, Hough parameters, dictionary indexing, reindexing, CI/IQ/MAD/fit/NCC, grain-level objectives, autonomous microscopy, and acquisition feedback. Patent searches returned no relevant EBSD patent in the searched corpus. Absence findings below therefore mean **“not found in this systematic search,” not a legal opinion of novelty or freedom to operate**.

| Area | Closest published work(s) | What is automated | Objective/criterion | What is explicitly not automated | Gap assessment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Optimizer-driven tuning of EBSD pattern-processing or indexing parameters | **Closest demonstrated EBSD parameter sweep:** Polonsky et al. 2019 parameterized DREAM.3D reconstruction variables and swept grain-segmentation misorientation tolerance over 0.1–10° in 0.1° increments, generating 100 reconstructions; **nearby but different:** Zhu et al. 2022 is only available here as metadata for “global optimization algorithms” applied to orientation/pattern-center/deformation extraction, so it should be treated as adjacent prior art, not verified from text in this record; **nearby non-tuning automation:** Kaufmann et al. 2020 CNN phase mapping automates phase recognition from patterns rather than tuning EBSD processing settings (polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 1-2, polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 5-6, kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 1-2, kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 6-7) | Automated batch execution / parameterization of reconstruction pipelines in BisQue+DREAM.3D; CNN-based direct phase classification from patterns in Kaufmann 2020 (polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 1-2, kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 1-2) | Polonsky used reconstruction-level metrics: fraction of “good” CI-masked voxels retained and total grain count, selecting an elbow/balance point at 2.0°; Kaufmann targets phase-map fidelity qualitatively against known microstructure/EDS, not optimizer search (polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 5-6, kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 6-7) | No evidence here of Bayesian optimization, Gaussian processes, genetic/evolutionary algorithms, RL, random/grid search over **pattern** processing settings such as background correction, binning, neighbor averaging, Hough band count, rho-theta smoothing, or dictionary settings. Polonsky optimizes segmentation/reconstruction variables after indexing, not indexing settings themselves. Kaufmann does not tune EBSD parameters at all (polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 5-6, kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 6-7) | **Gap largely open.** Closest evidence is reconstruction-pipeline parameterization, not closed-loop optimizer-driven tuning of pattern-processing/indexing knobs. |
| 2. Feedback loops that re-index stored raw patterns using CI/IQ/MAD/NCC to choose next parameter set | **Closest proposal:** Shen et al. 2019 proposes combining fast CNN predictions with a confidence measure (quaternion norm) so that high-confidence points get neighborhood dictionary search and low-confidence points get full dictionary search; **related raw-pattern availability, not loop:** Stinville et al. 2022 notes raw .up2 patterns can be opened in EMsoft DI / EMSphInx, enabling reindexing in principle (shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 10-12, shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 1-2, stinville2022multimodaldatasetof pages 9-12, stinville2022multimodaldatasetof pages 12-13) | Shen automates confidence estimation for each location and proposes routing subsequent dictionary matching effort based on confidence; raw pattern archival in Stinville enables offline reindexing workflows (shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 10-12, stinville2022multimodaldatasetof pages 12-13) | Quaternion norm as confidence proxy in Shen; no demonstrated CI/IQ/MAD/NCC-driven next-parameter selection loop in the gathered evidence (shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 10-12) | Shen does **not** demonstrate an executed closed loop that iteratively changes indexing/processing parameters and re-indexes stored raw patterns to maximize CI/IQ/MAD/NCC/NCC-like objectives; it is a proposed hybrid search allocation strategy. Stinville provides data access, not autonomous optimization (shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 10-12, stinville2022multimodaldatasetof pages 12-13) | **Gap open.** Proposal-level hybrid confidence routing exists, but not a demonstrated feedback optimizer that selects the next EBSD parameter set from reindexed raw patterns. |
| 3. Optimization against grain-level or microstructure-level outcomes | **Closest demonstrated:** Polonsky et al. 2019 explicitly optimizes a grain-segmentation parameter against microstructure-level outcomes (grain count and retained good-data fraction); Staněk et al. 2020 compares 2D/3D segmentation sensitivity to misorientation threshold and shows strong threshold dependence, but not autonomous optimization (polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 5-6, polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 6-8, stanek2020comparisonofsegmentation pages 1-2, stanek2020comparisonofsegmentation pages 7-9) | Automated parallel reconstructions and post-processing counts in Polonsky; analytical comparison of threshold effects on segmentation in Staněk (polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 5-6, stanek2020comparisonofsegmentation pages 1-2) | Grain count stability / avoidance of grain merging plus retained CI-masked voxel fraction in Polonsky; sensitivity of number of grains and segmentation discrepancies vs threshold in Staněk (polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 5-6, stanek2020comparisonofsegmentation pages 7-9) | No demonstrated multi-objective or constrained optimization over broader grain-level cleanup outcomes such as speckle/wild-grain fraction, grain-boundary integrity, fraction of pixels altered by cleanup, or Pareto balancing across multiple EBSD post-processing stages. Polonsky is a one-parameter sweep with manually interpreted elbow criterion (polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 5-6, polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 6-8) | **Partially occupied, but narrow.** Grain-level optimization exists for segmentation tolerance; broader autonomous multi-objective EBSD post-processing remains a gap. |
| 4. Hybrid Hough-first / dictionary-on-residue and automated escalation criteria | **Closest published work:** Shen et al. 2019 explicitly proposes a hybrid strategy: CNN preliminary prediction plus confidence, then pattern matching only in a neighborhood for high-confidence points and full dictionary search for low-confidence points; this is the clearest automated escalation criterion in the gathered evidence. Sparks et al. 2024 and Winiarski et al. 2021 automate registration/distortion correction workflows but not Hough→dictionary escalation (shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 10-12, sparks20243dreconstructionof pages 23-24, winiarski2021correctionofartefacts pages 15-17) | Automated confidence scoring and proposed routing of dictionary-search scope in Shen; automated image registration/distortion correction in Sparks/Winiarski (shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 10-12, sparks20243dreconstructionof pages 23-24, winiarski2021correctionofartefacts pages 15-17) | Criterion in Shen is confidence from quaternion norm: high confidence → local neighborhood dictionary search; low confidence → full dictionary search (shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 10-12) | No evidence in the gathered text of a **demonstrated** Hough-first then dictionary-on-low-quality-residue loop with automated escalation based on CI/IQ/MAD/NCC thresholds. Shen’s routing is proposed around CNN+dictionary, not Hough+dictionary, and not shown as an executed autonomous residue-reindexing pipeline (shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 10-12) | **Mostly gap.** There is a close proposal for automated escalation, but not a demonstrated Hough-residue-to-dictionary autonomous workflow. |
| 5. Autonomous/self-driving EBSD post-processing or characterization workflows, including links back to SEM acquisition recommendations | **Closest workflow automation:** Sparks et al. 2024 automates sample/image registration steps, pattern-center fitting for every section, and alignment routines; Winiarski et al. 2021 automates SE–EBSD distortion correction and argues more automated procedures are needed; Burnett et al. 2016 demonstrates a fully automated serial-sectioning routine with tracking fiducials, but acquisition settings were experimentally chosen; Kaufmann et al. 2020 automates phase mapping from patterns (sparks20243dreconstructionof pages 9-12, sparks20243dreconstructionof pages 23-24, winiarski2021correctionofartefacts pages 15-17, winiarski2021correctionofartefacts pages 4-6, burnett2016largevolumeserial pages 4-6, burnett2016largevolumeserial pages 6-7, kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 1-2) | Automated registration/warping, per-layer EBSD-to-BSE alignment, CI-threshold masks, pattern-center fitting per section, and automated serial sectioning with fiducial tracking; CNN inference for phase maps (sparks20243dreconstructionof pages 23-24, sparks20243dreconstructionof pages 9-12, burnett2016largevolumeserial pages 4-6, kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 1-2) | Workflow goals are geometric consistency, low inter-section misorientation, and corrected distortions; Burnett assesses equivalent quality via EBSD pattern quality/band contrast and indexing rate after experimentally selected settings (sparks20243dreconstructionof pages 9-12, winiarski2021correctionofartefacts pages 15-17, burnett2016largevolumeserial pages 6-7) | No evidence here of a human-out-of-the-loop EBSD post-processing system that autonomously tunes post-processing/indexing parameters end-to-end, nor of a loop that feeds post-processing outcomes back to SEM acquisition parameters such as beam current, dwell time, or step size. Burnett explicitly determines acceptable milling current experimentally; Winiarski says more automated procedures still need to be developed (burnett2016largevolumeserial pages 6-7, winiarski2021correctionofartefacts pages 15-17) | **Gap open.** Sub-workflow automation exists, but not a self-driving closed-loop EBSD characterization system that recommends or controls acquisition parameters from post-processing outcomes. |


*Table: This table maps the closest published prior art found for the five requested EBSD automation areas, distinguishing demonstrated methods from proposals and from absent closed loops. It highlights that most evidence clusters around workflow automation and grain-segmentation parameter sweeps, not autonomous closed-loop tuning of indexing/processing parameters.*

## 1. Optimizer-driven tuning of pattern-processing or indexing parameters

### Closest demonstrated work: Polonsky et al. (2019)

Polonsky and colleagues integrated DREAM.3D into the cloud-based BisQue platform so that pipeline variables could be parameterized and executions parallelized. Their principal EBSD example varied the **post-indexing grain-segmentation misorientation tolerance** from 0.1° to 10° in 0.1° increments, producing 100 three-dimensional reconstructions while holding minimum-neighbor and minimum-defect-size settings fixed. They evaluated the fraction of CI-masked “good” voxels retained and total reconstructed grain count, then selected 2.0° from convergence/elbow behavior in the derivatives of those metrics. This is genuine automated parameter sweeping with microstructure-level evaluation. However, it operates on already indexed orientation data; the study states that raw EBSD patterns were not collected for that dataset. It therefore does **not** tune background correction, detector binning, neighbor averaging, Hough band count, Hough rho/theta smoothing, or dictionary-search settings, and it cannot re-index patterns under candidate settings. (polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 1-2, polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 5-6, polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 6-8)

### Adjacent work that should not be overread

Shen et al. developed CNN-based orientation indexing and optimized neural-network architecture/training for speed and prediction accuracy. The trained model indexes patterns directly and uses quaternion-norm deviation as a reliability measure. This replaces or supplements conventional indexing; it does not run Bayesian, evolutionary, grid, or reinforcement-learning search over conventional EBSD processing parameters. It also remains sensitive to experimental geometry and requires detector/setup parameters to be determined beforehand or accommodated through retraining. (shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 1-2, shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 8-10, shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 10-12)

Kaufmann et al. automated phase classification from individual EBSD patterns with a CNN. The work reduces human decisions in phase mapping and outperforms conventional Hough-plus-user-selected phase/chemistry workflows in difficult examples. The “optimization” described for the conventional comparator was repeated **user adjustment** of EDS reference chemistry against a microstructure already known in advance, not an algorithmic search over EBSD settings. The CNN likewise classifies patterns rather than optimizing background, Hough, binning, or dictionary parameters. (kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 1-2, kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 6-7)

Global/evolutionary optimization has also been published for extracting or refining orientation, pattern center, and deformation state from pattern matching. That is important neighboring art: it establishes optimizer use **inside a per-pattern inverse problem**. It is not equivalent to an outer loop choosing data-processing/indexing hyperparameters from map-quality or grain-quality outcomes. The retrieved full-text evidence did not support treating such work as prior art for the broader closed-loop parameter-selection architecture.

**Assessment:** No verified publication was found that applies Bayesian optimization, a GP surrogate, genetic/evolutionary search, random/grid search, RL, or a comparable optimizer to the listed **pattern-processing and indexing knobs** and automatically selects the best configuration. Area 1 remains substantially open, aside from adjacent per-pattern refinement and post-indexing segmentation sweeps.

## 2. Re-indexing stored raw patterns in a metric-driven feedback loop

Stinville et al. provide a useful enabling precedent: their archived 3D dataset includes approximately 1.71 TB of raw `.up2` Kikuchi patterns, and the paper explicitly states that these can be opened and reprocessed with EMsoft dictionary indexing, EMSphInx spherical-pattern reindexing, or commercial EBSD software. The indexed files also expose IQ and CI. This demonstrates the technical availability of stored-pattern reindexing, but the paper is a dataset publication, not an optimizer: it does not generate candidate parameter sets, score them, or select the next experiment. (stinville2022multimodaldatasetof pages 9-12, stinville2022multimodaldatasetof pages 12-13)

Shen et al. provide the closest feedback-like decision rule. They propose obtaining a preliminary CNN orientation and confidence at every point, performing only a local dictionary search around high-confidence predictions, and performing a full dictionary search for low-confidence predictions. The confidence proxy is the norm of the predicted quaternion. This is automated computational routing, but it is not a demonstrated iterative loop over processing/indexing parameter sets, and it does not use CI, IQ, MAD/fit, or NCC to propose the next candidate configuration. (shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 10-12)

Polonsky et al. use CI to define an initial mask of good voxels and assess how many remain after cleanup and segmentation. CI is therefore part of a reconstruction-level quality assessment, but it is not fed back to re-index raw patterns; indeed, raw patterns were unavailable in that example. (polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 5-6)

**Assessment:** No demonstrated publication was found with the complete loop **candidate parameters → re-index stored raw patterns → compute CI/IQ/MAD/fit/NCC objective → choose the next parameter set → repeat**. Area 2 remains an unclaimed gap in the searched literature.

## 3. Grain- or microstructure-level objectives

This area has the strongest direct prior art, but it is narrow.

Polonsky et al. explicitly recognized that segmentation tolerance changes grain consolidation and retained data in opposite directions. Their two high-level metrics were total grain count and the fraction of initially CI-qualified voxels retained through reconstruction. They chose the lowest tolerance at which the changes in both quantities became approximately constant, analogous to an elbow criterion. This is a microstructure-level, effectively two-metric parameter-selection procedure rather than optimization of a per-pattern score. (polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 5-6, polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 6-8)

Staněk et al. independently show why such objectives matter. They analyzed the dependence of 2D and 3D grain segmentation on misorientation threshold, including mean grain counts and the formation of erroneously merged giant grains. For one noisy experimental dataset, changing noise removal and excluding grains below eight voxels changed the detected population from more than one million grains to 74,579. This is a systematic sensitivity study and supplies possible grain-level observables, but it does not implement an autonomous optimizer or select cleanup parameters through a formal multi-objective rule. (stanek2020comparisonofsegmentation pages 1-2, stanek2020comparisonofsegmentation pages 7-9)

Neither publication demonstrates optimization across a broad EBSD-processing chain using objectives such as wild-grain/speckle fraction, boundary continuity or integrity, grain-count stability over threshold perturbations, fraction of pixels modified by cleanup, or a constraint on topology preservation. Polonsky varies essentially one segmentation parameter, keeps other settings fixed, and identifies a balance/elbow rather than computing a Pareto front or solving a constrained optimization problem. (polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 5-6)

**Assessment:** Area 3 is **partially occupied**. A broad claim to “optimizing EBSD processing using grain-level outcomes” would encounter Polonsky et al. A narrower architecture that jointly tunes indexing and cleanup parameters using several topology- and intervention-aware grain objectives still appears open in the searched literature.

## 4. Hybrid Hough-first/dictionary-on-residue indexing

The closest automated escalation rule is Shen et al., but its first stage is a CNN rather than Hough indexing. Their proposed rule is explicit: high-confidence CNN results receive dictionary matching only near the preliminary orientation; low-confidence results receive full dictionary search. Thus, the publication anticipates confidence-triggered allocation of expensive pattern matching. It does not demonstrate a Hough-first pipeline, does not define residue using CI/IQ/MAD/NCC from Hough indexing, and does not report an executed end-to-end selective reindexing experiment. (shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 10-12)

The same paper compares CNN and Hough indexing at different exposure times. CNN indexing produced a larger fraction of points below a 10° misorientation-error cutoff at high noise, whereas Hough was more accurate among the smaller subset it indexed correctly. This comparison motivates selective hybridization, but the reported hybrid suggestion remains CNN-to-dictionary rather than Hough-to-dictionary. (shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 8-10, shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 10-12)

Kaufmann et al. likewise replace conventional Hough phase assignment with CNN classification; they do not retain Hough as a first pass and selectively escalate failed pixels. (kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 1-2, kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 6-7)

**Assessment:** Confidence-triggered hybrid search is neighboring prior art, so a very broad claim to “use confidence to decide whether to run dictionary matching” is not open. However, no verified demonstration was found of **Hough first → automatically identify low-quality residue → dictionary/pattern-match only that residue**, particularly using an explicit CI/IQ/MAD/NCC or grain-context escalation criterion. Area 4 therefore remains mostly open in the requested Hough-specific form.

## 5. Autonomous EBSD workflows and acquisition feedback

Several publications automate substantial sub-workflows:

* **BisQue–DREAM.3D:** cloud execution, provenance, parallel pipeline runs, and range parameterization for 3D reconstruction. Parameters and ranges are supplied rather than autonomously discovered, and the demonstrated optimization begins after indexing. (polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 1-2, polonsky2019threedimensionalanalysisand pages 5-6)
* **Automated serial sectioning:** Burnett et al. describe a fully automated PFIB serial-section routine using automatically recognized tracking fiducials and repeated milling/imaging positions. Yet acceptable milling current was determined experimentally, and the authors state that systematic mapping of voltage/current space remained necessary. EBSD settings—including beam energy/current, dwell, binning, band count, and Hough settings—were fixed by the investigators rather than adapted from post-processing results. (burnett2016largevolumeserial pages 4-6, burnett2016largevolumeserial pages 6-7)
* **Automated registration and distortion correction:** Sparks et al. use automated sample alignment, pattern-center fitting for each section, CI thresholding, and optimizer-based multimodal registration. The optimizer maximizes an image-registration similarity metric and transforms maps; it does not alter EBSD indexing settings or SEM acquisition conditions. (sparks20243dreconstructionof pages 9-12, sparks20243dreconstructionof pages 23-24)
* **SE–EBSD map correction:** Winiarski et al. automate aspects of co-registration and long-/short-range distortion correction using trainable filters and moving least squares. The paper explicitly concludes that more automated procedures and more robust accuracy measures still need development. It also discusses faster or smart acquisition as a prospect, not as a closed post-processing-to-acquisition controller. (winiarski2021correctionofartefacts pages 4-6, winiarski2021correctionofartefacts pages 15-17)
* **CNN indexing/phase mapping:** Shen and Kaufmann automate inference from patterns, but training data, instrument calibration, phase standards, and/or model selection remain external; neither closes the loop to microscope settings. (shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 1-2, shen2019convolutionalneuralnetworkbased pages 8-10, kaufmann2020phasemappingin pages 1-2)

No retrieved work used post-processing outcomes to recommend or automatically change **beam current, pattern dwell/exposure, detector binning, or spatial step size** for a subsequent SEM/EBSD acquisition. Burnett et al. come closest to connecting acquisition conditions with indexing rate and band contrast, but the comparison is an investigator-designed experiment, not a controller: selected ion currents are evaluated under fixed EBSD conditions and an acceptable current is chosen experimentally. (burnett2016largevolumeserial pages 4-6, burnett2016largevolumeserial pages 6-7)

**Assessment:** Automated components and scripted pipelines are well established, so “automated EBSD workflow” alone is not a gap. A genuinely autonomous, human-out-of-the-loop EBSD characterization system that interprets indexed/map/grain quality and then recommends or controls SEM acquisition parameters remains open in the searched literature.

## Consolidated gap assessment

1. **Optimizer-driven tuning of EBSD pattern-processing/indexing settings — open.** Neighboring art covers per-pattern inverse optimization, ML indexing, and post-indexing segmentation sweeps, but not outer-loop optimization of background, binning, averaging, Hough, or dictionary hyperparameters.
2. **Metric-driven iterative reindexing of stored raw patterns — open.** Raw-pattern reindexing is enabled and confidence-directed search is proposed, but the complete iterative objective loop was not found.
3. **Grain-level optimization — partially claimed.** Polonsky et al. directly cover segmentation-tolerance selection using retained-good-data fraction and grain count. Broad multi-objective, constrained, topology-aware optimization across indexing plus cleanup remains open.
4. **Automated hybrid escalation — partially anticipated, Hough-specific implementation open.** Shen et al. anticipate confidence-triggered local versus full dictionary search after CNN indexing. A demonstrated Hough-first, dictionary-on-residue workflow with formal escalation criteria was not found.
5. **Autonomous workflow with feedback to acquisition — open at the system level.** Serial sectioning, registration, reconstruction, correction, and ML inference are individually automated, but no end-to-end post-processing-to-SEM acquisition feedback system was found.

The most defensible unexplored combination is therefore: **repeated reindexing of archived raw patterns under optimizer-selected processing/indexing settings; joint pattern-, pixel-, and grain-level objectives with explicit cleanup/topology constraints; confidence- and grain-context-based escalation from Hough to dictionary matching; and translation of the optimized result into acquisition recommendations or microscope control.** None of the verified publications combines those elements into a closed, autonomous EBSD loop.

| Area | Closest published work(s) | What is automated | Objective/criterion | What is explicitly not automated | Gap assessment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Optimizer-driven tuning of EBSD pattern-processing or indexing parameters | **Closest demonstrated EBSD parameter sweep:** Polonsky et al. 2019 parameterized DREAM.3D reconstruction variables and swept grain-segmentation misorientation tolerance over 0.1–10° in 0.1° increments, generating 100 reconstructions; **nearby but different:** Zhu et al. 2022 is only available here as metadata for “global optimization algorithms” applied to orientation/pattern-center/deformation extraction, so it should be treated as adjacent prior art, not verified from text in this record; **nearby non-tuning automation:** Kaufmann et al. 2020 CNN phase mapping automates phase recognition from patterns rather than tuning EBSD processing settings (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005) | Automated batch execution / parameterization of reconstruction pipelines in BisQue+DREAM.3D; CNN-based direct phase classification from patterns in Kaufmann 2020 (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000004) | Polonsky used reconstruction-level metrics: fraction of “good” CI-masked voxels retained and total grain count, selecting an elbow/balance point at 2.0°; Kaufmann targets phase-map fidelity qualitatively against known microstructure/EDS, not optimizer search (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000005) | No evidence here of Bayesian optimization, Gaussian processes, genetic/evolutionary algorithms, RL, random/grid search over **pattern** processing settings such as background correction, binning, neighbor averaging, Hough band count, rho-theta smoothing, or dictionary settings. Polonsky optimizes segmentation/reconstruction variables after indexing, not indexing settings themselves. Kaufmann does not tune EBSD parameters at all (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000005) | **Gap largely open.** Closest evidence is reconstruction-pipeline parameterization, not closed-loop optimizer-driven tuning of pattern-processing/indexing knobs. |
| 2. Feedback loops that re-index stored raw patterns using CI/IQ/MAD/NCC to choose next parameter set | **Closest proposal:** Shen et al. 2019 proposes combining fast CNN predictions with a confidence measure (quaternion norm) so that high-confidence points get neighborhood dictionary search and low-confidence points get full dictionary search; **related raw-pattern availability, not loop:** Stinville et al. 2022 notes raw .up2 patterns can be opened in EMsoft DI / EMSphInx, enabling reindexing in principle (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003) | Shen automates confidence estimation for each location and proposes routing subsequent dictionary matching effort based on confidence; raw pattern archival in Stinville enables offline reindexing workflows (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000003) | Quaternion norm as confidence proxy in Shen; no demonstrated CI/IQ/MAD/NCC-driven next-parameter selection loop in the gathered evidence (pqac-00000017) | Shen does **not** demonstrate an executed closed loop that iteratively changes indexing/processing parameters and re-indexes stored raw patterns to maximize CI/IQ/MAD/NCC/NCC-like objectives; it is a proposed hybrid search allocation strategy. Stinville provides data access, not autonomous optimization (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000003) | **Gap open.** Proposal-level hybrid confidence routing exists, but not a demonstrated feedback optimizer that selects the next EBSD parameter set from reindexed raw patterns. |
| 3. Optimization against grain-level or microstructure-level outcomes | **Closest demonstrated:** Polonsky et al. 2019 explicitly optimizes a grain-segmentation parameter against microstructure-level outcomes (grain count and retained good-data fraction); Staněk et al. 2020 compares 2D/3D segmentation sensitivity to misorientation threshold and shows strong threshold dependence, but not autonomous optimization (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) | Automated parallel reconstructions and post-processing counts in Polonsky; analytical comparison of threshold effects on segmentation in Staněk (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000010) | Grain count stability / avoidance of grain merging plus retained CI-masked voxel fraction in Polonsky; sensitivity of number of grains and segmentation discrepancies vs threshold in Staněk (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000011) | No demonstrated multi-objective or constrained optimization over broader grain-level cleanup outcomes such as speckle/wild-grain fraction, grain-boundary integrity, fraction of pixels altered by cleanup, or Pareto balancing across multiple EBSD post-processing stages. Polonsky is a one-parameter sweep with manually interpreted elbow criterion (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000012) | **Partially occupied, but narrow.** Grain-level optimization exists for segmentation tolerance; broader autonomous multi-objective EBSD post-processing remains a gap. |
| 4. Hybrid Hough-first / dictionary-on-residue and automated escalation criteria | **Closest published work:** Shen et al. 2019 explicitly proposes a hybrid strategy: CNN preliminary prediction plus confidence, then pattern matching only in a neighborhood for high-confidence points and full dictionary search for low-confidence points; this is the clearest automated escalation criterion in the gathered evidence. Sparks et al. 2024 and Winiarski et al. 2021 automate registration/distortion correction workflows but not Hough→dictionary escalation (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000000, pqac-00000008) | Automated confidence scoring and proposed routing of dictionary-search scope in Shen; automated image registration/distortion correction in Sparks/Winiarski (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000000, pqac-00000008) | Criterion in Shen is confidence from quaternion norm: high confidence → local neighborhood dictionary search; low confidence → full dictionary search (pqac-00000017) | No evidence in the gathered text of a **demonstrated** Hough-first then dictionary-on-low-quality-residue loop with automated escalation based on CI/IQ/MAD/NCC thresholds. Shen’s routing is proposed around CNN+dictionary, not Hough+dictionary, and not shown as an executed autonomous residue-reindexing pipeline (pqac-00000017) | **Mostly gap.** There is a close proposal for automated escalation, but not a demonstrated Hough-residue-to-dictionary autonomous workflow. |
| 5. Autonomous/self-driving EBSD post-processing or characterization workflows, including links back to SEM acquisition recommendations | **Closest workflow automation:** Sparks et al. 2024 automates sample/image registration steps, pattern-center fitting for every section, and alignment routines; Winiarski et al. 2021 automates SE–EBSD distortion correction and argues more automated procedures are needed; Burnett et al. 2016 demonstrates a fully automated serial-sectioning routine with tracking fiducials, but acquisition settings were experimentally chosen; Kaufmann et al. 2020 automates phase mapping from patterns (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000000, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000004) | Automated registration/warping, per-layer EBSD-to-BSE alignment, CI-threshold masks, pattern-center fitting per section, and automated serial sectioning with fiducial tracking; CNN inference for phase maps (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000004) | Workflow goals are geometric consistency, low inter-section misorientation, and corrected distortions; Burnett assesses equivalent quality via EBSD pattern quality/band contrast and indexing rate after experimentally selected settings (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000007) | No evidence here of a human-out-of-the-loop EBSD post-processing system that autonomously tunes post-processing/indexing parameters end-to-end, nor of a loop that feeds post-processing outcomes back to SEM acquisition parameters such as beam current, dwell time, or step size. Burnett explicitly determines acceptable milling current experimentally; Winiarski says more automated procedures still need to be developed (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008) | **Gap open.** Sub-workflow automation exists, but not a self-driving closed-loop EBSD characterization system that recommends or controls acquisition parameters from post-processing outcomes. |


*Table: This table maps the closest published prior art found for the five requested EBSD automation areas, distinguishing demonstrated methods from proposals and from absent closed loops. It highlights that most evidence clusters around workflow automation and grain-segmentation parameter sweeps, not autonomous closed-loop tuning of indexing/processing parameters.*

info.query:
Systematic prior-art survey: closed-loop, automated, or algorithm-driven optimization of EBSD (electron backscatter diffraction) data-processing and indexing parameters.

Specifically map what has been published on:
1. Automated or optimizer-driven tuning of EBSD pattern-processing or indexing parameters (background correction, binning, neighbour averaging, Hough transform settings such as band count / rho-theta smoothing, dictionary indexing settings), using Bayesian optimization, Gaussian processes, genetic/evolutionary algorithms, grid/random search, or reinforcement learning.
